title: Learning Assistant Supported Student Outcomes (LASSO) study initial findings
extended_summary:
This paper reports initial findings from the LASSO study, which examines how characteristics of Learning Assistant (LA)-supported STEM courses are associated with student learning outcomes. The central question is whether student, course, and instructor features predict gains on concept inventories in LA-supported classes, and whether patterns differ by gender, race, interaction time with LAs, and instructor experience using LAs.

The study analyzed pre/post concept inventory data from over 4,500 students and 17 instructors across 13 LA Alliance member institutions. Faculty completed questionnaires about course structure and LA use, while students reported demographics and time spent interacting with LAs. Outcomes were measured using concept inventories in physics, biology, and chemistry, with hierarchical linear models used to account for nesting of students within courses. The analysis also compared outcomes across disciplines and among student subgroups.

The main findings were that higher student interaction time with LAs was associated with larger learning gains up to a point, and that more instructor experience teaching a course with LAs was associated with better student outcomes. At the same time, the paper reports gender and racial differences in learning gains, suggesting inequities remain in LA-supported classrooms. Because the work is correlational and based on the first semester of a multi-year dataset, the authors emphasize that causal claims cannot be made and that further research is needed to isolate which LA practices are most effective.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational multi-institution observational study using hierarchical linear models, but it is not experimental and cannot establish causality. The paper provides useful subgroup and contextual evidence, but credibility is limited by self-selection, missing demographics for a large subset, and reliance on pre/post concept inventories.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports medium-sized learning gains overall (grand mean d=0.845) and a notable positive association between student-LA interaction and outcomes, which suggests meaningful impact in science courses. Because the evidence is correlational and not directly about K-12 Khanmigo-like tutoring, the impact is promising but not definitive.

finding.finding_summary: In this correlational multi-institution study of LA-supported science courses, students showed average pre-post gains on concept inventories, with a grand mean effect size of d=0.845 across 3,315 usable paired responses. However, gains varied substantially by discipline/instrument (e.g., FMCE d=1.230, BEMA d=1.130, CCI d=0.052), and the paper does not attribute these gains to a specific technology intervention beyond the LA-supported instructional context.
finding.measure: Pre/post science concept inventory scores (FMCE, BEMA, CINS, GCA, IMCA, CCI, GCIICS)
finding.effect_size: d=0.845 (grand mean); instrument-level d ranged 0.052 to 1.248

finding.finding_summary: Student interaction time with LAs was positively associated with larger learning gains up to 16–30 minutes/week, where that group had average effect sizes of 0.873 versus 0.369 for students reporting 0 minutes/week. The paper interprets the 30+ minute group as possibly reflecting selection effects among struggling students, so the pattern is positive but not uniformly increasing.
finding.measure: Self-reported weekly interaction time with Learning Assistants and associated pre/post concept inventory effect sizes
finding.study_size: n=3315 overall; interaction-time model used subgroup counts ranging from n=184 to n=318
finding.effect_size: d=0.873 for 16–30 min/week vs d=0.369 for 0 min/week; continuous slope not reported as standardized effect size

finding.finding_summary: The study found that more time spent interacting with LAs and more faculty experience teaching with LAs were associated with higher student learning gains, suggesting improved collaboration and sustained instructional support over time. For faculty experience, each additional term teaching the course with LAs was associated with a 0.154 increase in student effect size (p<0.05) across n=17 courses.
finding.measure: Student concept inventory gain effect sizes modeled against student-LA interaction time, student/LA ratio, faculty co-planning time, and faculty experience with LAs
finding.study_size: n=17 courses for course-level models; n=3315 for student-level analyses
finding.effect_size: 0.154 per additional term teaching the course with LAs; -0.005 per additional student/LA ratio; +0.004 per additional faculty minute/week meeting with LAs

finding.finding_summary: Across 13 institutions and 17 LA-supported courses, the study found inequitable outcomes by gender and race: male students had substantially higher average effect sizes than female students (0.749 vs 0.485), while white students outperformed Asian and 'other' students, with black students somewhat higher than white students. The authors frame these as correlational inequities in LA-supported classrooms and note that the findings motivate further work on equity and institutional practice.
finding.measure: Pre/post concept inventory effect sizes disaggregated by gender and race across LA-supported courses
finding.study_size: n=3315 usable pre-post pairs; n=17 courses; 13 institutions
finding.effect_size: Gender: 0.749 male vs 0.485 female; Race: 0.619 white vs 0.557 Asian, 0.669 black, 0.509 other
